welcome.title: Before You Start
body: This is not a quiz. There are no right answers. There is no winning.
What this is, is an invitation. An invitation to ask each other the questions you stopped asking. To remember why you chose each other. To make room for what God is still building in your marriage.
Pull one card. Read it aloud. Take turns answering. Listen all the way through before you respond. Stay soft.
Some questions will be easy. Some will open something you did not know was closed. Both are good.

instructions.title: How to Play Lovers Quest
steps: Shuffle the deck. Either of you can go first.
Draw one card. Read the question aloud.
The person who drew answers first. Take your time. Speak from where you actually are, not where you think you should be.
When you finish answering, ask your spouse, "What would you add?" Then they answer.
Before moving to the next card, take three seconds of silence together. Let what was said settle.
When you are done for the night, set the deck aside. Pick up again next time.
ground_rules: Do not use a card as a weapon.
Do not bring up an old fight while answering.
Do not check your phone between cards.
instructions.final_note: If a question is too hard for tonight, set it aside. There is no requirement to answer every card the same evening. Real conversation is not a race.

completion.title: You've reached the end of the deck.
completion.subtitle: Some marriages drift. Yours does not.
completion.note: Take a minute before you put it down. What came up tonight that is worth carrying into the week?

about.tagline: Some marriages drift. Yours does not have to.
about.body: Lovers Quest is a faith-rooted card game for couples who refuse to let their marriage run on autopilot. 72 honest questions across six dimensions of how you love each other: Intimacy, Trust, Purpose, Conflict, Grace, and Legacy.
about.credit: A Spiritual Romeo Production. By Dennis Nickens.

categories.name: Intimacy
categories.description: The flame represents what's burning between you. Not just physical intimacy, but the closeness of being fully known and fully chosen.

categories.name: Trust
categories.description: The key represents what's locked between you. Trust is the access you grant each other to the parts of yourself you protect from everyone else.

categories.name: Purpose
categories.description: The compass represents where you are headed together. Marriage is not just two people. It is a direction. This is the category that pulls you toward what God is building.

categories.name: Conflict
categories.description: The hand offering the leaf represents the fight FOR each other instead of AGAINST each other. Every marriage has conflict. The question is whether yours moves you toward each other or pulls you apart.

categories.name: Grace
categories.description: The rose represents the beauty that grows in soil that has been broken open. Grace is not just forgiveness. It is the soft place you give each other to land when you are not at your best.

categories.name: Legacy
categories.description: The crown represents what outlives you both. The love story you write together will keep speaking long after you stop. This category asks what you want it to say.

cards.text: When did you feel most known by me?
cards.context:
This one asks about a specific moment, not a general feeling. Think about a recent time where your spouse saw something in you that no one else would have caught. Not what they said about it. What you felt when you realized they saw it.

The point isn't to find the perfect example. It's to put words to what being known by your spouse actually feels like, so they know which way to keep moving.

cards.text: What do you wish I would ask you more often?
cards.context:
People remember which questions their spouse never asks. The absence of a question can land harder than a hard conversation. This is your chance to name what you've been waiting to be asked, without making your spouse feel like they should have known.

Speak it softly. The point isn't to indict them for not asking. It's to give them the question, so they can ask it now and going forward.

cards.text: When was the last time you felt fully wanted by me, and how did I show it?
cards.context:
There's a difference between feeling tolerated, feeling appreciated, and feeling actually wanted. Wanted means they chose you in a moment they could have chosen something else. Think about a recent time that landed for you that way.

Name the specifics of what they did. The HOW matters as much as the WHAT. Naming the specifics teaches them how to do it again.

cards.text: What part of you do you think I have stopped seeing?
cards.context:
Long marriages slowly stop noticing. The parts of you they fell in love with don't disappear, but their attention to them can. This question asks you to point at something specific, not to complain.

A trait, a gift, a softness, a strength. Something that's still there but isn't being seen lately. The point is to put it back on their radar so they can choose to look again.

cards.text: What does it feel like to be loved by me right now?
cards.context:
Right now, not in your wedding video. The way they love you has changed over the years, and so has the way you love them. This question asks you to describe the actual texture of being loved by them today.

Safe? Quiet? Distracted? Steady? Whatever the honest word is. They cannot adjust what you do not name.

cards.text: When you need to feel close to me but cannot find the words, what would help?
cards.context:
Closeness sometimes asks for words. Sometimes it asks for something else entirely. A look. A hand on the back. A few minutes on the couch with no agenda. This question asks you to describe the non-verbal language that actually reaches you.

Most spouses default to talking when their partner needs something else. Tell them what the something else looks like.

cards.text: What is one thing about how we love each other that you never want to lose?
cards.context:
Marriages lose things slowly, sometimes without noticing. Some habits and rhythms between you are sacred and worth protecting before they fade.

Name one. Not the obvious one. The small specific one only the two of you would notice. The point is to put a stake in the ground so neither of you accidentally lets it go.

cards.text: When was the last time we were intimate that you felt was about US, and not just about being intimate?
cards.context:
Physical intimacy can be about a lot of things. Sometimes it's just release. Sometimes it's connection. Sometimes one person is fully present and the other is somewhere else.

This asks for a specific recent moment where you both knew it was about the two of you, not just the act. If you can't think of one, that's worth saying too. Without blame.

cards.text: What is the most intimate moment we have had in the last six months that did not involve our bodies?
cards.context:
Intimacy isn't only physical, and the most intimate moments between spouses sometimes happen fully clothed in the kitchen. A conversation that went somewhere unexpected. A look across the room when something hard was happening. A silence that meant more than words.

Name a moment, and what made it land that way for you.

cards.text: What about the way we used to be close do you miss, and what about how we are close now do you not want to give up?
cards.context:
This is a both-and question. Marriages evolve, and what you miss is real, and what you've gained is real. Both halves matter. Don't let yourself only answer one.

Name one thing from earlier that you wish was still part of how you love each other. Then name one thing that's developed since that you would not trade back.

cards.text: What part of you do you keep walled off, even from me, and what would it take for you to let me in?
cards.context:
Every person has rooms in them they keep closed. Some of those walls are old self-protection. Some are loyalty to a private version of yourself.

This asks you to name one of them honestly, without obligating yourself to take the wall down tonight. Then describe what would help you eventually let your spouse in. Naming the wall is the first step. Removing it is a separate conversation.

cards.text: When I look at you, what do you wish I saw that I am not seeing?
cards.context:
Spouses develop a fixed picture of each other over the years. Sometimes that picture stops updating. There's a version of you that exists now that they might not be tracking. A change. A growth. A wound you're still working on.

Tell them what you wish their picture of you included. The point isn't to argue with their view, it's to help them see you as you actually are today.

cards.text: What would help you feel safer being fully yourself with me?
cards.context:
Safety in a marriage isn't physical safety, it's permission to bring the whole self to the table. Most spouses still edit themselves a little, even after years.

Think about what you'd stop editing if you knew it would land softly. Then describe what your spouse would need to do (or stop doing) for that to be the case. Be specific. Vague safety is hard to provide.

cards.text: Is there something you have been carrying alone that I should know about?
cards.context:
Long marriages accidentally develop "things one of us is handling." Sometimes that's fine. Sometimes it's a weight one of you has been carrying that the other one would have happily helped with if they'd known.

This is your chance to put that thing on the table. Not as a complaint. As an invitation to share the load.

cards.text: When have I broken trust with you in a small way that you have not told me about?
cards.context:
Big trust breaks get talked about. Small ones get buried, and over time they add up to something bigger than the original violation.

This is your chance to surface one of those small ones safely. Not to assign blame. To clear the air. Speak it as something you've been carrying, not something they did to you. The goal is for both of you to know what's been sitting under the surface, so you can decide together what to do with it.

cards.text: What does trust look like to you in this season of our marriage, that did not look the same before?
cards.context:
The trust required in early marriage isn't the same as the trust required ten years in. As the seasons shift (kids, jobs, health, callings), what you need to feel safe with each other shifts too.

This asks you to describe what trust LOOKS like for you right now, not what it looked like five years ago. The form of it has probably changed. Name the current shape.

cards.text: Where do you need me to be more dependable, and what does that look like in practice?
cards.context:
"Be more dependable" is too vague to act on. This question asks for the specific area and the specific behavior.

A morning rhythm. A weekly check-in. Following through on a small recurring thing. Make it concrete enough that your spouse can do it on purpose. Reliability is built in specifics, not in general intentions.

cards.text: What would I have to do for you to feel completely safe sharing your hardest thoughts with me?
cards.context:
There's a difference between thoughts you tell your spouse and thoughts you keep to yourself because you've decided they can't hold them.

This asks you to describe what they'd have to do (or stop doing) for the held-back thoughts to feel safe to share. Often it's about their reaction, not their advice. They need to know that before they can offer it.

cards.text: When you do not trust me with something, what is the fear underneath that?
cards.context:
Lack of trust usually has fear sitting under it. Fear of being judged. Fear of being misunderstood. Fear of opening something that can't be closed.

This asks you to name the fear, not just the lack of trust. Once your spouse can see the fear, they can speak to it. Without the fear named, all they can do is feel rejected.

cards.text: Is there a financial decision we have made together that you have not been fully honest about how you feel?
cards.context:
Money decisions are some of the easiest places to silently disagree and never bring it up. A purchase you went along with. A budget choice you didn't push back on. A long-term plan you have private doubts about.

This is your chance to name it honestly, without revisiting the decision yet. First put the truth on the table. The decision itself can be revisited later if it needs to be.

cards.text: What is something I do or have done that makes you wonder if I am the same person you said yes to?
cards.context:
Marriages span seasons, and both spouses change. Sometimes a change is good. Sometimes it makes the other person wonder where the person they married went.

This is a hard question on purpose. Speak it without weaponizing it. The goal isn't to accuse them of being a stranger, it's to name what's shifted so the two of you can decide together whether to lean in or lean back.

cards.text: What is one trust I have rebuilt with you that you still secretly question, and what do you need from me to fully let it go?
cards.context:
Rebuilt trust often has a residue. Even when you've decided to forgive, a small part of you stays alert. This asks you to name that residue honestly.

Then describe what they could do (or what time they'd need to demonstrate consistency) for the residue to dissolve. Speak it as information they can act on, not as an accusation.

cards.text: Where in our marriage are you carrying something alone because you do not believe I can handle it?
cards.context:
Some weights get carried alone because we've decided our spouse can't bear them. Sometimes that's protection. Sometimes that's a quiet judgment about who they are.

This question invites you to name where you've made that call, and to consider whether you're underestimating them. They may be ready to carry more than you've given them credit for.

cards.text: What is the thing I would need to do today for you to feel like I am completely on your side?
cards.context:
Spouses can be on each other's side in general and still leave moments where the other one doesn't feel it.

This asks for a specific present-tense action. Not a year-long change. One thing they could do today, this week, that would land in your body as "they have my back." Make it concrete. Make it something they could actually do.

cards.text: What is God inviting us to build together?
cards.context:
Marriage is a partnership and most partnerships have a build, a shared assignment, a thing the two of you are uniquely positioned to do.

This asks you to put words to what you sense God is asking of you AS A COUPLE, not just as individuals. It doesn't have to be big. It doesn't have to be public. It just has to be true.

cards.text: If we lived the next ten years the way we have lived the last two, where would we end up?
cards.context:
This question doesn't ask for hope, it asks for trajectory. Where does the math of your current habits, rhythms, and choices actually land you in a decade?

Be honest. If the answer is somewhere you don't want to be, that's information. If it's somewhere you do want to be, that's confirmation. Either way, name it specifically.

cards.text: What do you think we are uniquely positioned to do as a couple that no other couple in our circle can do?
cards.context:
There's an assignment with your name on it that nobody else can fulfill the same way. The combination of who you both are, what you've been through, who you have access to, what you've learned makes a unique offering.

This asks you to name what that is, even if it feels presumptuous. Especially if it feels presumptuous.

cards.text: What is one assignment you sense God has put on our marriage, that we have not stepped into yet?
cards.context:
Most couples can name something they've felt called to that they haven't yet acted on. Fear, timing, finances, doubt.

This is your chance to name it out loud, even if you can't act on it tonight. Naming it is the first step toward stepping into it. Don't let another season pass with this one unspoken.

cards.text: Where do you feel called that I have not fully gotten behind you on?
cards.context:
One spouse can be sensing something the other one hasn't fully seen or supported yet. Maybe a calling, a ministry, a career direction, a personal growth path.

This asks you to name where that gap is, not as a grievance, but as a request for them to look again. Sometimes spouses just need to know what they've been missing in order to step in.

cards.text: What is the version of us you most want to see in five years, and what is in the way of that?
cards.context:
This asks two questions. First, picture the version of the two of you that you most want to grow into. Be specific. Not "happier," but a real picture.

Then name what's currently between you and that version. A pattern. A fear. A choice you keep avoiding. The future version is reachable, but only if you name the obstacle and decide to do something about it.

cards.text: When you imagine the legacy God wants from this marriage, what is the first image that comes up?
cards.context:
Don't think too hard. The first image is usually the truest one. It might be your kids. It might be a stage. It might be a quiet meal table with people you've poured into.

Whatever flashes first, describe it. Then describe what would have to be true in your marriage today for that image to actually become real.

cards.text: What is something you are sensing God wants from you that you are afraid to tell me, because you do not know how it would change us?
cards.context:
Some callings come to one spouse first, and they sit on them because they're afraid of what it would mean for the marriage. A move. A career shift. A ministry. A change in lifestyle.

This is your chance to put it on the table. Not as a decision. As something you've been carrying alone that you need help thinking about with the person you're going to do it with.

cards.text: If we had to choose between two callings, one for each of us, that would not both fit in the same season, how would we decide together?
cards.context:
Marriages eventually face moments where you can't both have what you sense. Whose dream takes priority? Whose calling waits?

This question asks you to think about your decision-making process BEFORE you're in the heat of it. What values would you use? What conversation would you have? Building the framework now makes the actual decision easier later.

cards.text: What are we putting time and money into right now that you suspect is not part of what we are actually called to build?
cards.context:
Most couples have at least one drain they suspect is misaligned but haven't named. A commitment, a relationship, a subscription, a habit.

This is the chance to name it honestly without yet deciding what to do about it. Sometimes naming is enough to start shifting it.

cards.text: When was the last time you felt God spoke directly to you about us as a couple, and did you tell me what you heard?
cards.context:
God speaks. Sometimes to one spouse, sometimes to both. Sometimes the one who heard kept it to themselves because they weren't sure how to share it.

This asks you to bring that word into the room. Not as a debate. As something the two of you need to hold together, since the marriage was the subject.

cards.text: What is the assignment I have been resisting, that you have already seen and have been waiting for me to step into?
cards.context:
Sometimes one spouse sees a calling on the other one before the other one is ready to admit it's there.

This flips the question. You're asking your spouse what they've been seeing in you that you haven't been willing to claim yet. Listen carefully. They may be naming something true. The fact that you've resisted it doesn't mean it isn't yours.

cards.text: How do you want us to fight for each other, not against each other?
cards.context:
Healthy couples still fight. The difference is the direction of the fight.

This asks you to describe what fighting FOR each other actually looks like in real time. Specific behaviors. A pause before reacting. A phrase that signals you're both on the same team. The framework only works if you've defined it in advance.

cards.text: What is the pattern in our disagreements that you wish would change?
cards.context:
Conflict in a marriage is usually patterned. The same dance, the same triggers, the same escalation. This asks you to name the pattern from your perspective, not to assign blame.

Once both of you can see the same pattern, you can both interrupt it. Patterns are easier to break when both people know the choreography.

cards.text: When we are in conflict, what do you need from me that you rarely ask for?
cards.context:
In the middle of a fight, most people don't know how to ask for what they need. They need space and ask for distance. They need to be held and ask for an apology.

This asks you to name, in calm, what you actually need in heat. Then your spouse will know what to give next time.

cards.text: What is something I do during arguments that makes it harder for you to hear me?
cards.context:
Some behaviors shut your spouse down before your words even land. Tone, volume, body language, a phrase that triggers them.

This asks you to name one specific thing they do that closes you off. Not the whole list. One thing. They can address one thing.

cards.text: Is there an old wound between us that has never fully healed, and what would healing it look like?
cards.context:
Most marriages carry at least one wound that got bandaged but never fully closed. It comes up sideways in unrelated fights.

This is your chance to name it AND describe what healing it would actually look like. Not just "an apology." The actual texture of what closure would feel like for you.

cards.text: What is one thing I could say in the middle of a hard moment that would help you feel safe?
cards.context:
A single phrase, said at the right moment, can de-escalate a fight. What's yours? Not what should be theirs.

What's the line that, if your spouse said it to you mid-conflict, would let you exhale? Tell them. They cannot say what they don't know to say.

cards.text: When was the last time we had a fight that brought us closer, and what was different about it?
cards.context:
Not all fights damage the marriage. Some of them actually deepen it. This asks you to think back to one that ended in more closeness than you started with.

What was different about it? The timing? The honesty? The willingness to hear before responding? Naming what worked teaches you both how to do it again.

cards.text: When we fight while we are exhausted, what do I do that makes it harder, and what could I do instead?
cards.context:
Exhausted fights aren't real fights, but the damage from them is real.

This asks you to name your spouse's exhaustion pattern (theirs, not yours) and offer an alternative behavior they could choose. Give them a script. "When we're both tired and you do X, it lands harder. If you could Y instead, that would help." That's actionable.

cards.text: Who is usually the first to repair after a fight between us, and is that the way we both want it, or have we both gotten used to it?
cards.context:
Most couples have one spouse who consistently makes the first move to reconcile. Sometimes that's their gift. Sometimes it's a habit that lets the other one off the hook.

This asks you to look at the pattern honestly. Is it still working for both of you? Or is it time to redistribute the labor of repair?

cards.text: What is the conflict between us we keep avoiding, even though we both know it is sitting there?
cards.context:
Every marriage has at least one conversation both people know is needed and both people keep stepping around.

This is the chance to name it without yet having it. Just put the topic on the table. The actual conversation can happen later. Naming what you're avoiding is half the work of stopping the avoidance.

cards.text: When my family of origin shows up in our fights, what pattern do you wish I would acknowledge before we have to keep fighting it?
cards.context:
We all bring our families into our marriages. Some of those patterns are gifts. Some of them are landmines.

This asks your spouse to name a specific pattern from your family of origin that they wish you would recognize on your own, before it has to be pointed out for the hundredth time. Hear them. Don't defend the family. Listen to what they're saying about the pattern.

cards.text: When is your silence harder for me than your words, and how do I tell the difference between you needing space and you needing me to follow?
cards.context:
Silence in marriage means many things, and most spouses misread it at least some of the time.

This asks you to help your spouse decode yours. When does your silence mean "give me room?" When does it mean "come find me?" Without the decoder, they'll guess wrong half the time and you'll feel unseen for it.

cards.text: Where do you need more grace from me right now?
cards.context:
Grace isn't a general topic, it's a specific present-tense need. There's a place in your life right now where you need your spouse to extend you something softer than what you're getting.

Maybe in how they react to your mistakes. Maybe in how patient they are with your growth. Maybe in how they hold a struggle of yours. Name the place. Be specific.

cards.text: What is something you have not been able to forgive yourself for that you wish I would help you carry?
cards.context:
Some weights we put on ourselves can't be put down without help. A failure, a mistake, a season we're ashamed of.

This is your chance to name yours, not to be absolved, but so your spouse can stand with you in the carrying. Sometimes that's all it takes for the weight to start to shift.

cards.text: When have I given you grace in a way that changed something in you?
cards.context:
This is a thank-you in question form. There was a moment where your spouse extended you grace you didn't expect, and something in you shifted because of it.

Name it. Tell them what it did for you. The point isn't to pay them back. It's to let them know that the grace landed somewhere real.

cards.text: What does grace look like to you when you have hurt me, and how do I extend it well?
cards.context:
This is the harder direction. When you've been the one who hurt them, you need a specific kind of grace from them, not generic forgiveness but a particular shape of welcome back.

This asks you to describe what that looks like FOR YOU. Then your spouse will know how to offer it the next time you mess up, which (let's be honest) is coming.

cards.text: Is there a part of yourself you keep apologizing for, that I want you to know does not need apology?
cards.context:
Most spouses have something they reflexively apologize for that their partner actually loves about them, or at least doesn't mind.

This flips the script. Listen for what your spouse names. Their answer is permission to stop apologizing. Receive it.

cards.text: What does it cost you to stay soft with me, and how can I make it easier?
cards.context:
Softness in marriage isn't free. It costs energy, especially when the other person is going through something hard.

This asks you to name what staying soft is currently costing you, and what your spouse could do to lighten that cost. Soft isn't sustainable on its own. It needs support to keep being soft.

cards.text: When you mess up, what kind of response from me actually helps you become better?
cards.context:
Different responses from a spouse produce different outcomes. Some make you defensive. Some make you ashamed. Some make you want to grow.

This asks you to describe what kind of response actually leads to the growth your spouse wants for you. Then they have a roadmap for the next time you mess up.

cards.text: What does grace look like in our marriage on the days we do not feel like extending it to each other?
cards.context:
Grace on a good day is easy. Grace on a hard day is the actual practice.

This asks you to describe what grace looks like specifically on the days when neither of you wants to give it. The minimum viable version. The version that gets you through without becoming someone who withholds. Define it now, while you're calm. Use it when you're not.

cards.text: What is something you have already forgiven me for that I do not even know you had to forgive?
cards.context:
Some grace gets extended quietly. Your spouse forgave you for something and never mentioned it.

This is the chance to surface one of those, not to make them feel bad, but to acknowledge what's already been done. Then the air clears. Some things don't need to be re-litigated. They just need to be named.

cards.text: Is there grace you have been withholding from me that you are starting to realize I have been waiting for?
cards.context:
Sometimes one spouse is holding back forgiveness or softness, and the other one is quietly waiting for it. This is hard.

You're asked to look at where you've been withholding, name it honestly, and notice what it's been costing your spouse to wait. This isn't a request to release it tonight. It's a request to admit it's been held.

cards.text: What would it look like for you to receive my grace fully, instead of holding part of yourself back to prove you do not need it?
cards.context:
Receiving grace is harder than extending it for a lot of people. There's pride in it.

This asks you to consider where you've been refusing your spouse's grace in order to prove you can do it on your own. Then describe what fully receiving would look like. It's not weakness to take what's offered.

cards.text: What grace does our marriage itself need from both of us right now, separate from the grace we extend each other?
cards.context:
Sometimes the marriage as a thing needs grace too. Not from one spouse to the other. From both of you to the relationship itself.

Maybe patience while it's adjusting. Maybe mercy during a hard chapter. This asks you to name what the marriage needs from both of you collectively, not what either of you needs individually.

cards.text: What kind of love story do you want us to leave behind?
cards.context:
Your marriage is going to be a story someone tells eventually. To your kids. To other couples. To people who watched it.

This asks you to describe the version of that story you want told. Not the polished version. The true version that includes what you want the takeaway to be. Name it now and you have something to live toward.

cards.text: If our children, or the people who watched us, were to describe our marriage in one sentence, what would you want them to say?
cards.context:
One sentence forces you to choose. Not five things. The one thing you most want people to remember about how you two loved each other.

Say it out loud. Then notice if your current life is making that sentence true. If not, what would need to shift?

cards.text: What is one thing about how we love each other that you hope sets a standard for the next generation?
cards.context:
Marriages set standards whether they mean to or not. Your kids, your nieces and nephews, the younger couples in your circle. They're watching how you handle each other.

This asks you to name the one thing you most want them to take as the standard. Then you can be intentional about modeling it.

cards.text: What is something we have been through together that you would not trade for an easier story?
cards.context:
Some chapters were hard but they built something between you that couldn't have been built any other way.

This asks you to name one. Not to romanticize the hard part. To recognize what the hard chapter actually gave you that you wouldn't give back.

cards.text: When we are old and looking back on this season, what do you want to remember about us?
cards.context:
You're going to be old together. That's the assumption this question is built on. The season you're in right now will look very different in 30 years.

So zoom out. What about this exact chapter (the kids being young, the business being new, the season being hard, whatever it is) do you want your future selves to remember? Not what you'll be proud of. What you'll be glad you didn't miss.

cards.text: What is the prayer you most often pray over us, and what would it look like to step into that prayer more fully?
cards.context:
There's a prayer you keep coming back to about your marriage. Maybe protection. Maybe peace. Maybe direction.

This asks you to name it, then ask what it would look like to live as if God were already answering it. Sometimes the prayer is the assignment.

cards.text: If God called you home tomorrow, what would you want me to know about what our marriage gave you?
cards.context:
This question is heavy on purpose. It asks you to think about what you'd want your spouse to carry forward about what the marriage meant to you, if you weren't here to keep telling them.

Don't rush past this one. The answer is what makes the marriage holy.

cards.text: What legacy is our marriage already leaving in our extended family, that we have not named out loud but that everyone around us can see?
cards.context:
Sometimes the people watching see what the people inside don't. Your marriage is already doing something for your siblings, your cousins, your parents, your kids.

This asks you to consider what that legacy already is. Name it. Then decide if you want to lean into it on purpose.

cards.text: When our children or the people we are raising remember what marriage looked like in this house, what do you most want them to remember?
cards.context:
Children remember texture more than they remember events. They remember whether their parents touched each other in the kitchen, whether they laughed, whether they fought softly or loud.

This asks you to name the specific texture you most want them to carry into their own marriages. Then make sure your house has it.

cards.text: What failure in our marriage became part of our story, that we would tell another couple about if we were ever asked to share something real?
cards.context:
Every honest marriage has a failure or a near-failure that became part of how it grew. Not the polished version. The one you'd actually tell a young couple if they asked.

This asks you to name yours together. Then decide whether the two of you are ready to start telling that story to people who need to hear it.

cards.text: What faith inheritance specifically do you want our marriage to leave behind, that you are not sure we are actually building yet?
cards.context:
There's something spiritual you want to leave behind that you haven't yet built. A practice. A standard. A way of seeing God together.

This asks you to name what's missing, and consider what would have to change for it to actually become part of your legacy. The legacy you leave is the legacy you build on purpose.

cards.text: If our marriage were a book that someone wrote about us in 50 years, what chapter title would describe the season we are in right now?
cards.context:
Zoom out one more time. Look at the chapter you're currently in. Give it a title, the kind that captures what's true about this season for you both.

Maybe it's "The Hard Year." Maybe it's "When We Finally Got Honest." Maybe it's "The Beginning of the Build." Title it. Then ask what you want the next chapter to be called.
